records.name: Côte d'Ivoire
records.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 the country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city (Abidjan).

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying NYT article (Oct 2024) covers the situation of LGBTQ people in Ivory Coast (Côte d'Ivoire).

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation/prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and inclusion of LGBT+ people.

US State Department 2023 report, Côte d'Ivoire: same-sex conduct not criminalised, but LGBTQI+ persons faced violence — three community deaths reported in the year; police responses to non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim; a transgender man was beaten in Abobo, Abidjan, while walking with another man. Authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Côte d'Ivoire: post-electoral-crisis context (3,000 deaths, sexual violence, displacement) - general human-rights baseline with limited LGBT-specific content.

Critical African Studies (2015), Thomann & Corey-Boulet, 'Violence, Exclusion and Resilience among Ivoirian Travestis': travestis (born anatomically male, living as women) face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention, and have been underserved by Ivoirian rights groups that distanced themselves from them; examines isolation after the 2010-11 post-election violence.

Same article via PMC canonical URL (Thomann & Corey-Boulet 2015): the key academic source on trans-feminine people's experiences in Côte d'Ivoire — documented violence and social exclusion of travestis alongside their resilience; duplicate of the ncbi copy retained as canonical mirror.

records.name: Mali
records.summary:
Mali is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (6 November 2024): Mali’s new penal code criminalises same-sex conduct with harsh penalties; previously legal but vague "public indecency" provisions (Article 225) were used against LGBT people and gender-nonconforming expressions, and the new law bans the undefined "promotion" of homosexuality, greatly expanding who can be prosecuted.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Mali's new criminalisation of same-sex conduct.

The Conversation (15 January 2025), interview with anthropologist Christophe Broqua: Mali’s new penal code — announced October 2024, in force 13 December 2024 — criminalises homosexuality and any citizen seen to encourage it, a sharp escalation under the military junta alongside clampdowns on opposition and media.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Mali: official assessment - same-sex conduct not criminalised but significant societal stigma; violence and instability from armed groups.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Mali: documents gender inequality, FGM, corruption, and 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' among other human-rights problems.

records.name: Mozambique
records.summary:
Mozambique demands real caution from trans visitors — one of Africa's better legal positions. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 Penal Code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register (Lambda Mozambique); and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. Counterweights: no legal gender recognition, no SOGI hate-crime statute, social hostility outside Maputo is significant, and the Cabo Delgado insurgency affects the north (a general, not trans-specific, risk).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest infrastructure; avoid the north.

sources.summary: Outright International (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct legal since the 2015 penal code; no legal gender recognition procedure exists; societal attitudes broadly neutral but LGBTIQ people face family ostracisation and employment/education barriers; the 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations then disappointed. Freshness confirmed: the new 2024 penal code removed the employment non-discrimination protection that had existed.

GlobalGayz archive (2006-2011): dated milestones — first newspaper article arguing gay rights (Agencia de Informacao, 7 July 2006), Maputo men petitioning parliament, the LGBT group still unregistered as of March 2011, refugee deaths en route to South Africa; documents early organising under the colonial-era law.
Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2016) from Afrobarometer: Mozambique among Africa's more tolerant — 56% would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour (vs Uganda/Burkina Faso/Niger at 5%).

Global Voices (28 Nov 2017): after a decade of blocked applications (since 2008), the Constitutional Council — supreme court equivalent — ruled Lambda Mozambique's status did not violate the constitution, unblocking registration of the country's only LGBT organisation.

Guardian (30 June 2015): Mozambique's new penal code erased the colonial 'vices against nature' provision; Lambda (not yet officially registered at the time) pivoted to anti-discrimination lobbying; Lambda's Carina Capitine: the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries but does face discrimination.

records.name: Rwanda
records.summary:
Rwanda demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations).

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and the constitution recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman — a partner-travel consideration for a trans visitor.

sources.summary: Outright International Rwanda overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, but the Human Rights First Rwanda Association's 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuses against transgender people — harassment at identity checks and arbitrary arrests on 'vagrancy'/'public order' grounds; LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, a public Pride event was held in 2021, and NGO Law No. 058/2024 (adopted June 2024) raises freedom-of-association concerns.

Vice (20 Nov 2020): reports violent detentions of transgender people in Rwanda: On Christmas day in 2018, Bella was walking out of a hotel in Kigali, Rwanda’s capital city, where she had been booked to sing for the holiday. After her show, she celebrated with friends and enjoyed the afternoon at the hotel bar. Stepping onto the street to make her way home, Bella— whose name has been changed due to concerns for her safety—was stopped by police officers. “I had my service card that showed I was working ther

KT Press (25 Sep 2016): asked at Rwanda Cultural Day in San Francisco about LGBT life in Rwanda, President Kagame replied 'it hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem'; the piece cites Article 26 of the constitution, which recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman.

Queerstory Files blog (8 Oct 2012): historical overview of the Great Lakes region — anthropologists report that same-sex relations among young Tutsi and Hutu men existed pre-colonisation but were private and secret; situates Rwanda alongside Uganda and Burundi (independence 1962) and post-1994 genocide memory. Background/history, not current visitor risk.

records.name: Angola
records.summary: Angola demands real caution from trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.

sources.summary: Shadow report on Angola's compliance with the African Charter, submitted for the African Commission's 81st session (Oct-Nov 2024, Banjul) by Angolan organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA, Diversidade Masculina and others) with ILGA/Synergia support: documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people in Angola.

Submission by Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights pre-session (74th, review of Angola): foregrounds the Angolan context for lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people ahead of the state's review — a formal international-review channel raising discrimination and health-access issues.

Southern Africa Litigation Centre chapter 'Transgender Rights in Angola': maps constitutional protection gaps — Article 23 does not list gender or sexual orientation as prohibited discrimination grounds — and locates identity, privacy, liberty, torture-protection and expression rights across Title II articles of the Angolan Constitution.

VICE continental overview (Oct 28, 2019): Angola singled out as having gone furthest among African reforms — not only removing the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision but also criminalising discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and services; contrasts legislative drafting strategies across the continent.

BBC profile (Apr 12, 2012): kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, becomes a mainstream star at 25 in what the article describes as a Catholic country where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour — evidence of visible trans presence alongside formal criminalisation at that time.

PinkNews (Feb 11, 2021): Angola's decriminalisation took effect on this date — the law adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era ban describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and made discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds punishable by prison.

records.name: Zambia
records.summary:
Zambia is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) with documented recent enforcement: Amnesty International's November 2024 campaign highlights Madalitso Zulu, serving a 15-year sentence with hard labour; Amnesty's 2024 regional report documents rising hostility in Zambia. There is no legal gender recognition, religious leaders lead anti-LGBT mobilisation, and police are perpetrators more than protectors.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest; the documented serving-sentence case shows courts impose maximum terms.

sources.summary: Amnesty International campaign story (26 Nov 2024) 'Madalitso's story': a Zambian medical professional —36, three years behind bars by Nov 2024 — imprisoned for consensual same-sex conduct; his medical expertise lost to a health system short of workers; frames individual persecution of LGBTI people in Zambia.

US State Dept 2021 Country Report, Zambia: government continued to reject recognition/protection of LGBTQI+ rights; police perpetrated violence and verbal/physical harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation; LGBTQI+ people at risk of societal violence from prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of law; advocacy groups report police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTQI+ individuals (fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha / $30-$900); discrimination in employment, housing, education and health continued.

HRW report 'Dignity Debased' (12 Jul 2016): documents forced anal examinations in at least eight countries including ZAMBIA — less frequent there than Egypt/Tunisia but prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal exams as court evidence in sodomy cases (incl. a mass trial of ~20 men); recommends worldwide ban; such exams are treated by victims as painful, degrading sexual violence.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Zambia: no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons; when police detain LGBTQI+ members they often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release; no credible reports of government agents condoning violence, but President Hichilema's 30 May statement opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults; societal violence and employment/housing/education/health discrimination continued.
